title: Questions 168-171 refer to the following article.
passage_1:
Galashiels (14 March)—In a former mill on the outskirts of town, Isobel Frayne, the owner of Windrow Weaving, runs a workshop devoted to reproducing historic cloth. The workshop’s reputation is wide, drawing designers and museum staff from across the country and even from abroad.

Ms. Frayne is often asked why she refuses to use modern synthetic yarn. Her answer is short: “Cloth should age the way the original did.” She insists on hand-spun wool coloured with plant dyes in order to keep the soft handle of the finished web.

Recently, Rufus Okonkwo, a curator at the National Textile Collection, praised Ms. Frayne’s work online, showing a seventeenth-century coverlet she had meticulously restored for a coming exhibition. The endorsement has brought a rush of inquiries, proving that hand skills still have a place in an age of machines.
